documentation='Radial neutral-particle convection velocity is the effective coefficient of the density-proportional advective flux of neutral particles in edge-plasma transport. It represents directed drift, pinch, or outward convection after density-gradient-driven diffusive transport has been separated.

The radial convective particle flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{n,r}^{\mathrm{conv}} = n_n v_{n,r}
$$

where $\Gamma_{n,r}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the radial particle flux due to convection, $n_n$ is the neutral-particle number density, and $v_{n,r}$ is this radial convection velocity.

The quantity applies to the neutral-particle channel in the edge plasma and is the radial component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is an effective coefficient for the named neutral-particle population, not a sum of energy or momentum transport coefficients.

The quantity excludes density-gradient-driven diffusive transport and is distinct from the full [neutral_particle_convection_velocity](name:neutral_particle_convection_velocity), which has no directional projection. The [parallel_neutral_particle_convection_velocity](name:parallel_neutral_particle_convection_velocity) represents the corresponding projection along the magnetic field rather than along increasing major radius.

documentation='Toroidal magnetic field at a flux surface is the coefficient $B_\phi$ multiplying $\hat{\phi}$ in the cylindrical decomposition of the equilibrium magnetic-field vector at a point on a selected magnetic flux surface. The direction $\hat{\phi}$ belongs to the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis, where $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

The component is the signed scalar projection onto the toroidal basis vector:

$$

documentation='Y direction unit-vector component of a neutron detector is the signed projection, in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, of the unit vector directed from a field-of-view voxel center toward the detector center. It is the y direction cosine of that line-of-sight direction.

The component is defined by projecting the detector-directed unit vector onto the $\hat{y}$ basis vector:

$$
u_y = \hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathrm{det}} \cdot \hat{y} = \frac{(\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{det}} - \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{vox}}) \cdot \hat{y}}{\lVert \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{det}} - \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{vox}} \rVert}
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathrm{det}}$ is the unit vector from the field-of-view voxel center to the detector center, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{det}}$ is the detector-center position, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{vox}}$ is the field-of-view voxel-center position, and $\hat{y}$ is the y basis vector of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

This quantity is a signed direction-cosine component, not a position coordinate, distance, or unnormalized displacement component. Together with the corresponding x and z components it satisfies $u_x^2 + u_y^2 + u_z^2 = 1$ when the field-of-view voxel center and detector center are distinct.'; source_paths=['neutron_diagnostic/detector/field_of_view/direction_to_detector/y']

documentation='The alpha angle is the signed inclination of the first axis of an oblique, trapezoidal or parallelogram-shaped cross-section of one passive conductor loop element. It specifies the orientation of that element’s cross-sectional geometry in the poloidal plane.

The angle is defined from the directed first-axis vector:

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_1 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}},\,\mathbf{a}_1 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\right)
$$

where $\alpha$ is the alpha inclination angle, $\mathbf{a}_1$ is the directed first axis of the cross-section, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the outward radial unit vector, $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the upward vertical unit vector, and $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the signed angle from the radial component to the vertical component. These directions are defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies independently to each passive loop element and to its own oblique cross-section; it is not an aggregate angle for a complete passive loop or a collection of elements. It describes the first cross-sectional axis only, not the transverse dimensions of the element and not the overall loop reference-axis inclination represented by the [tilt angle of the passive loop](name:tilt_angle_of_passive_loop). The alpha angle supplies orientation information for interpreting the element’s other cross-sectional geometry, but does not determine those dimensions.

Sign convention: Positive when the first axis rotates counterclockwise from the outward radial direction toward the positive vertical direction in the poloidal plane.'; dd_source_docs=[{'id': 'pf_passive/loop/element/geometry/oblique/alpha', 'unit': 'rad', 'description': 'First inclination angle (alpha, α) of the oblique (trapezoidal/parallelogram) cross-sectional geometry of a passive conductor loop element, measured counter-clockwise from the outboard horizontal. $$
v_\phi(\mathbf{x}_m)=\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{imp}}(\mathbf{x}_m)\cdot\hat{\phi}
$$

For an impurity population combined over charge states, the bulk velocity is the density-weighted mean over the included charge states. The species and charge-state aggregation must be interpreted from the defined population; the related [toroidal ion velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity) provides the corresponding generic ion quantity.

Sign convention: Positive when the impurity-ion flow points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.'; source_paths=['mhd/ggd/velocity_phi/values']

documentation='The rate at which particles of the electron-equivalent population are removed from the plasma region by wall pumping is the global scalar representation of the wall particle-removal flux. It describes pumped particle exhaust using equivalent-electron counting rather than a local wall flux density.

The global removal rate is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{e,\mathrm{pump}} = \frac{dN_{e,\mathrm{removed}}}{dt}
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,\mathrm{pump}}$ is the pumped particle-removal rate expressed in equivalent electrons, $N_{e,\mathrm{removed}}$ is the cumulative number of electron equivalents removed by wall pumping, and $t$ is time.

This quantity is aggregated over the wall and represents the total pumping throughput for the electron-equivalent population. The electron-equivalent basis does not assert that all removed particles are physical electrons, and the quantity is not an areal flux density, an electrical current, or a rate for one specified neutral species.

It is the electron-specific specialization of the general [particle-removal flux at the wall due to pumping](name:particle_rate_at_wall_due_to_pumping). documentation='The toroidal ion charge-state momentum convection velocity is the $\phi$-component of the effective velocity vector $\mathbf{v}_c^{(s)}$ appearing in the non-diffusive term of the charge-state-resolved fluid momentum transport equation for ion charge state $s$:

$$
v_{c,\phi}^{(s)} = \hat{\phi} \cdot \mathbf{v}_c^{(s)}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and $\mathbf{v}_c^{(s)}$ is the effective momentum convection velocity vector for charge state $s$.

This quantity is charge-state-resolved and is distinct from [toroidal_ion_momentum_convection_velocity](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_convection_velocity), which provides the corresponding quantity aggregated over all charge states of a species. It is one projection component of the [ion_charge_state_momentum_convection_velocity](name:ion_charge_state_momentum_convection_velocity) vector family. As a transport coefficient in a convection-diffusion closure, it is not in general equal to the mean toroidal fluid velocity of the charge state.

Sign convention: Positive when $v_{c,\phi}^{(s)}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.'; source_paths=['edge_profiles/ggd/ion/state/velocity/phi', 'plasma_transport/model/profiles_1d/ion/state/momentum/toroidal/v', 'plasma_profiles/profiles_1d/ion/state/velocity/toroidal', 'plasma_profiles/ggd/ion/state/velocity/phi', 'plasma_transport/model/ggd/ion/state/momentum/v/phi', 'core_profiles/profiles_1d/ion/state/velocity/toroidal', 'edge_profiles/profiles_1d/ion/state/velocity/toroidal', 'core_transport/model/profiles_1d/ion/state/momentum/toroidal/v', 'edge_transport/model/ggd/ion/state/momentum/v/phi']

documentation='First-orbit-loss power is the kinetic-energy loss rate carried away by fast ions whose first guiding-center orbit after birth or acceleration intersects the confining boundary. It represents the aggregate loss from the confined fast-ion population, rather than energy transferred by collisions or subsequent orbit evolution.

The volume-integrated loss power is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{FOL}} = \int_V p_{\mathrm{FOL}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{x}
$$

documentation="The ion energy diffusion coefficient $D_{i,E}$ quantifies gradient-driven diffusive transport of thermal energy carried by the ion population, providing the Fick's-law proportionality between the density-normalized diffusive ion heat flux and the local ion temperature gradient. It is the ion-population specialization of the general [energy diffusion coefficient](name:energy_diffusion_coefficient) and is distinct from convective or $E \times B$ contributions to the total ion heat flux. As an intensive species-level coefficient, the total-ion value is the density-weighted mean over all ion species and charge states; [ion charge-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:ion_charge_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient) denotes the corresponding coefficient for a specified ion charge state.

The defining Fickian relation for the diffusive ion thermal-energy flux $\mathbf{Q}_{i,\mathrm{diff}}$ is:

$$
\mathbf{Q}_{i,\mathrm{diff}} = - n_i D_{i,E} \nabla T_i
$$

where $\mathbf{Q}_{i,\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive ion thermal-energy flux, $n_i$ is the total ion number density, $D_{i,E}$ is the ion energy diffusion coefficient, $T_i$ is the total-ion temperature expressed as thermal energy per ion, and $\nabla T_i$ is its spatial gradient. For ion species and charge-state components indexed by $a$, $n_i = \sum_a n_a$, $T_i = \sum_a n_a T_a / n_i$, and the intensive aggregation convention for component coefficients $D_{a,E}$ is $D_{i,E} = \sum_a n_a D_{a,E}/n_i$. The leading minus sign encodes down-gradient Fickian diffusion: for positive $D_{i,E}$, the diffusive flux points opposite to $\nabla T_i$.

This name is direction-agnostic. documentation='The parallel heat-viscosity current density is the field-aligned component of the electric current density generated when heat-viscosity terms in a collisional magnetized-plasma fluid closure drive net charge transport. It is the parallel projection of the parent [heat-viscosity current density](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity).

The defining projection is

$$
j_{\mathrm{hv},\parallel}=\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}}\cdot\mathbf{b}, \qquad \mathbf{b}=\frac{\mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}}$ is the heat-viscosity current-density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic-field vector, $|\mathbf{B}|$ is its magnitude, and $\mathbf{b}$ is the corresponding unit vector.

This quantity includes only the heat-viscosity mechanism and field-aligned projection; [parallel current density due to parallel viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) represents a distinct viscosity contribution.

Sign convention: Positive when the heat-viscosity current density points along the local magnetic-field direction $\mathbf{B}$.'; source_paths=['plasma_profiles/ggd/j_heat_viscosity/parallel', 'edge_profiles/ggd/j_heat_viscosity/parallel']

documentation='Imaginary part of the radial perturbed plasma magnetic field is the imaginary component of the complex first-order magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the confined plasma. It applies to one toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis and to the radial coordinate component in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

The complex radial component is decomposed into real and imaginary parts as:

$$
\delta B_{\rho}^{(n)}(\rho,\theta) = \delta B_{\rho,\mathrm{re}}^{(n)}(\rho,\theta) + i\,\delta B_{\rho,\mathrm{im}}^{(n)}(\rho,\theta)
$$

where $\delta B_{\rho}^{(n)}$ is the radial flux-coordinate component of the complex perturbed magnetic-field eigenfunction for toroidal mode number $n$, $\delta B_{\rho,\mathrm{re}}^{(n)}$ is the corresponding [real part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part), $\delta B_{\rho,\mathrm{im}}^{(n)}$ is this quantity, $i$ is the imaginary unit, $\rho$ is the radial flux coordinate, and $\theta$ is the poloidal flux coordinate.

The scope is the confined-plasma region for the specified toroidal mode; it excludes the perturbed magnetic field in the vacuum region, any sum over toroidal mode numbers, and any real-valued instantaneous perturbation obtained after applying a toroidal and temporal phase factor. The radial direction here is the coordinate direction associated with increasing $\rho$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$; it is distinct from the major-radius $\hat{R}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity is a local eigenfunction component, not a flux-surface average, volume integral, or magnitude.

Together with the [real part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part), this quantity forms the complex radial component $\delta B_{\rho}^{(n)}$. Together with the [poloidal](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part) and [toroidal](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part) imaginary components, it forms the imaginary vector part of the perturbed plasma magnetic-field eigenfunction. The overall complex phase of a linear eigenfunction is arbitrary, so a phase rotation mixes the real and imaginary parts while leaving the represented complex eigenfunction unchanged.

documentation='This quantity is the stiff implicit linear coefficient of the energy source or sink for the applicable ion population. It represents the temperature-dependent part of the ion energy source that is treated implicitly during time integration.

The implicit ion energy-source contribution is defined by

$$
S_{E,i}^{\mathrm{imp}} = \alpha_{E,i}^{\mathrm{imp}} T_i
$$

where $S_{E,i}^{\mathrm{imp}}$ is the implicit ion energy source contribution, $\alpha_{E,i}^{\mathrm{imp}}$ is this source-rate coefficient, $T_i$ is the local ion temperature, and the superscript $\mathrm{imp}$ denotes the implicit contribution. The subscript $E$ identifies the energy channel and $i$ identifies the applicable ion population.

The coefficient applies to the ion-species member represented by the ion channel; it is not summed over all ion species, does not represent a total-ion quantity, and does not select a particular ion charge state. It belongs to the energy channel and is distinct from particle- and momentum-source coefficients. The explicit, non-stiff remainder of the ion energy source is excluded. $$

documentation='Net conventional electric current delivered by the plasma to one divertor target surface is the signed charge-flow rate crossing the plasma-facing target interface, integrated over the wetted strike zone. It represents the net incident conventional current carried by charged plasma particles to that target.

The target current is defined by the surface integral of incident conventional-current density over the wetted target region:

$$
I_{\mathrm{target}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{wet}}} \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{inc}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{target}} \, dA
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{target}}$ is the current at the divertor target, $S_{\mathrm{wet}}$ is the wetted strike-zone part of the target surface, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{inc}}$ is the incident conventional electric-current density due to plasma particles at the target surface, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{target}}$ is the unit normal directed from the plasma into the target material, and $dA$ is the surface area element. For multiple charged species, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{inc}}$ is the charge-weighted sum of their incident particle flux densities, so ion and electron contributions enter with opposite electric-charge signs.

The scope is one physical divertor target surface; the aggregation convention is the surface integral over the wetted strike-zone region of that target. It excludes neighboring targets, non-target plasma-facing components, and return currents in external conducting structures. It is a net conventional current, not an ion-only current, an electron-only current, an unsigned collected-current magnitude, or a particle flux.

Summing this quantity over the target surfaces belonging to a divertor gives the target-current contribution to [current of divertor](name:current_of_divertor). If a target is partitioned into tiles, summing [current of divertor tile](name:current_of_divertor_tile) over the tiles that cover the same wetted target region gives this per-target quantity.

documentation='Ion charge-state energy flux at the wall due to recombination quantifies the rate at which recombination-associated energy from incident plasma ions of a specified species and charge state leaves a plasma-facing surface per unit area. It is the ion-associated component for that incident-ion population, not the incident plasma energy flux or heat deposited in the wall material.

The ion charge-state recombination energy flux at wall location $\mathbf{x}_w$ for incident species $i$ and charge state $\zeta$ is defined as the product-energy moment of the outgoing ion-associated recombination source:

$$
Q^{\mathrm{ion}}_{\mathrm{rec},i,\zeta}(\mathbf{x}_w) = \sum_{c,\,a,\,k}\int E_\mathrm{out}\,\frac{d\Gamma^{\mathrm{ion}}_{i,\zeta,c,a,k}}{dE_\mathrm{out}}(\mathbf{x}_w,E_\mathrm{out})\,dE_\mathrm{out}
$$

where $i$ identifies the incident-ion species, $\zeta$ the incident-ion charge state, $c$ an ion-associated surface recombination or neutralization channel, $a$ the emitted product species, $k$ the product internal state or emission class, $E_\mathrm{out}$ the energy carried into the plasma-facing half-space by an emitted product or quantum, and $d\Gamma^{\mathrm{ion}}_{i,\zeta,c,a,k}/dE_\mathrm{out}$ the corresponding outgoing recombination-product flux distribution with respect to product energy. documentation='Ion charge-state energy flux at the wall due to recombination quantifies the rate at which recombination-associated energy from incident plasma ions of a specified species and charge state leaves a plasma-facing surface per unit area. It is the ion-associated component for that incident-ion population, not the incident plasma energy flux or heat deposited in the wall material.

The ion charge-state recombination energy flux at wall location $\mathbf{x}_w$ for incident species $i$ and charge state $\zeta$ is defined as the product-energy moment of the outgoing ion-associated recombination source:

$$
Q^{\mathrm{ion}}_{\mathrm{rec},i,\zeta}(\mathbf{x}_w) = \sum_{c,\,a,\,k}\int E_\mathrm{out}\,\frac{d\Gamma^{\mathrm{ion}}_{i,\zeta,c,a,k}}{dE_\mathrm{out}}(\mathbf{x}_w,E_\mathrm{out})\,dE_\mathrm{out}
$$

where $i$ identifies the incident-ion species, $\zeta$ the incident-ion charge state, $c$ an ion-associated surface recombination or neutralization channel, $a$ the emitted product species, $k$ the product internal state or emission class, $E_\mathrm{out}$ the energy carried into the plasma-facing half-space by an emitted product or quantum, and $d\Gamma^{\mathrm{ion}}_{i,\zeta,c,a,k}/dE_\mathrm{out}$ the corresponding outgoing recombination-product flux distribution with respect to product energy. For discrete product energies, the integral is replaced by the corresponding sum.

This quantity resolves the incident-ion species and charge state within the ion-associated recombination energy channel. Summing over incident-ion charge states and incident-ion species gives [ion energy flux at the wall due to recombination](name:ion_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination); the broader [energy flux at the wall due to recombination](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination) also includes recombination energy channels outside this ion-associated component. It is the energy-weighted counterpart of [particle flux at the wall due to recombination] for the same surface recombination source.'; source_paths=['wall/description_ggd/ggd/energy_fluxes/recombination/ion/state/incident/values', 'wall/description_ggd/ggd/energy_fluxes/recombination/ion/state/emitted/values']

documentation='The electron energy convection velocity is the effective advection coefficient $V_{E,e}$ that parameterizes the convective, non-diffusive component of electron thermal-energy transport. It is distinct from the bulk plasma fluid velocity and represents the coefficient associated with drift and pinch contributions.

$$
Q_{\mathrm{conv},e} = \tfrac{3}{2} n_e T_e V_{E,e}
$$

where $Q_{\mathrm{conv},e}$ is the convective electron-energy flux, $n_e$ is the electron number density, $T_e$ is the electron temperature expressed as an energy, and $V_{E,e}$ is the electron energy convection velocity.

This is the electron-specific member of the [energy convection velocity] family and does not impose a radial or field-parallel projection. documentation='Toroidal component of electric current density carried by co-passing fast particles is the $\hat{\phi}$ component, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with $R$ major radius, $\phi$ toroidal angle, $Z$ vertical height, and $\hat{\phi}$ the direction of increasing $\phi$, of the electric current density due directly to fast nonthermal charged particles on co-passing untrapped guiding-center orbits. A co-passing orbit is an untrapped guiding-center orbit whose toroidal circulation is in the co-current direction, the direction of the plasma current.

The kinetic definition at position $\mathbf{r}$ is:

$$
J_{\phi,\mathrm{fast,co}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_s q_s \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}} v_\phi\, f_{s,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $J_{\phi,\mathrm{fast,co}}$ denotes this toroidal co-passing fast current-density component, $\mathbf{r}$ is position, $s$ labels fast-particle species, $q_s$ is the signed electric charge of species $s$, $v_\phi$ is the signed toroidal velocity component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $f_{s,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast-particle velocity-space distribution for species $s$, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $d^3v$ is the differential volume element in velocity space, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}$ is the co-passing region of velocity space.

Only the direct current carried by fast particles within $\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}$ is included. Thermal-electron and thermal-ion compensating return currents caused by momentum exchange with fast particles are excluded, as are counter-passing fast particles, trapped fast particles, and unrelated bulk-plasma current. The aggregation is a sum over the represented fast-particle species and over the co-passing velocity-space region; it is not a sum over thermal return-current carriers.

This scalar is the toroidal component of [co-passing fast current density](name:co_passing_fast_current_density). It is distinct from [toroidal co-passing current density](name:toroidal_co_passing_fast_current_density), which includes associated electron and thermal-ion return-current terms. The complementary orbit-class components are [toroidal counter-passing fast current density](name:toroidal_counter_passing_fast_current_density) and [toroidal trapped fast current density](name:toroidal_trapped_fast_current_density); their sum with this component gives [toroidal fast-particle current density](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_fast_ion) after applying the same spatial aggregation. A flux-surface-averaged value is the magnetic-flux-surface average of this same direct fast-particle toroidal component and does not change the included particle population.

Sign convention: Positive when the co-passing fast-particle current density flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.'; source_paths=['distributions/distribution/profiles_2d/co_passing/current_fast_phi', 'distributions/distribution/profiles_1d/co_passing/current_fast_phi', 'distributions/distribution/profiles_1d/co_passing/current_phi', 'distributions/distribution/profiles_2d/co_passing/current_phi']

documentation='Conventional electric current of a divertor tile is the net signed charge current crossing the electrostatic sheath from the plasma onto the plasma-facing surface of one individual divertor tile. It is a tile-level incident sheath current, expressed using the direction of conventional electric current rather than electron particle flow.

The current is the sheath-normal surface integral of the conventional electric current density over the tile surface:

$$
I_\mathrm{tile} = \int_{S_\mathrm{tile}} \mathbf{j} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{p}\to\mathrm{tile}} \, dS
$$

where $I_\mathrm{tile}$ is the conventional electric current of the divertor tile, $S_\mathrm{tile}$ is the plasma-facing surface of that tile, $\mathbf{j}$ is the conventional electric current density, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{p}\to\mathrm{tile}}$ is the surface normal directed from the plasma toward the tile, and $dS$ is the surface-area element.

The scope is one individual divertor tile and the aggregation is the net charge-weighted contribution of all charged species crossing the sheath onto that tile surface. It is not the current of a complete divertor target, not the current of an entire divertor, and not an electrical-conduction current in supports or external circuitry after charge has entered the solid.

The [current at a divertor target](name:current_at_divertor_target) is obtained by summing this quantity over the divertor tiles that constitute that target. The [current of a divertor](name:current_of_divertor) is obtained by summing the corresponding tile or target contributions over the divertor.

documentation='The flux-surface-averaged toroidal xenon velocity at the plasma boundary quantifies the mean azimuthal flow of xenon impurity ions around the torus, averaged along the last closed flux surface (separatrix). Xenon ($Z=54$) is a heavy noble-gas impurity used in radiative-mantle experiments to spread divertor heat loads, and its toroidal rotation reflects momentum balance between collisional coupling to the bulk plasma, neoclassical forces, and external toroidal momentum input.

The flux-surface average of the toroidal velocity component $v_\phi^\mathrm{Xe}$ is defined as:

$$
\langle v_\phi^\mathrm{Xe} \rangle = \frac{\oint v_\phi^\mathrm{Xe} \, B_p^{-1} \, dl}{\oint B_p^{-1} \, dl}
$$

where $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic field magnitude and the line integrals are taken along the plasma boundary contour.

Toroidal impurity velocities at the separatrix are measured primarily by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), resolving Doppler shifts from charge exchange between injected neutral beam atoms and Xe ions; a poloidally distributed array of sightlines is necessary to reconstruct the flux-surface average. The non-averaged counterpart is given by [toroidal_xenon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_xenon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), while analogous averaged quantities for lighter seeding species include [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_toroidal_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) and [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_argon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_toroidal_argon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).

documentation='The polarization angle at a constraint position is the angle of linear polarization of Stark-split Balmer-alpha emission from fast neutral beam ions traversing the plasma, evaluated at a discrete spatial site where this measurement serves as an input constraint in equilibrium reconstruction. The motional Stark effect (MSE) diagnostic exploits the Lorentz electric field experienced by injected beam neutrals to align the polarization plane of the emitted light in a direction encoding the local magnetic-field pitch angle.

The MSE polarization angle $\gamma$ is related to the local magnetic field components by:

$$
\tan(\gamma) = \frac{B_Z}{A_1 B_R + A_2 B_\phi}
$$

where $B_Z$ is the vertical field component, $B_R$ is the radial field component, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal field component, and $A_1$, $A_2$ are dimensionless geometric weighting factors determined by the beam trajectory and sightline orientation.

During equilibrium reconstruction, the measured value at each constraint position is compared against the corresponding reconstructed [polarization_angle](name:polarization_angle_at_constraint_position) to form residuals that enter the least-squares cost functional. The motional_stark_radiance provides complementary spectral intensity data from the same beam-emission event. MSE polarization angles in conventional-aspect-ratio tokamak configurations span a few degrees to roughly 20 degrees, varying with local field pitch, beam geometry, and viewing-sightline angle.'; documentation='Parallel fast-particle pressure is the field-aligned component of the kinetic pressure tensor carried by suprathermal particles. It is the all-orbit contribution to [fast-particle pressure], complementary to the transverse [perpendicular fast-particle pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_particle_pressure).

The flux-surface-averaged pressure is defined by the parallel second velocity moment:

$$
P_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}(\psi)=\left\langle \sum_s m_s\int v_\parallel^2 f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v\right\rangle_\psi
$$

where $\psi$ labels the magnetic flux surface, $\langle\cdot\rangle_\psi$ denotes its flux-surface average, $s$ labels fast-particle species, $m_s$ is particle mass, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is velocity, $v_\parallel=\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{b}$ is velocity along the magnetic-field unit vector $\mathbf{b}$, and $f_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the distribution function.

All guiding-center orbit classes are included, including co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped particles. The associated scalar trace satisfies $P_{\mathrm{fast}}=(P_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}+2P_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}})/3$; an orbit-restricted counterpart is [parallel co-passing fast-particle pressure](name:parallel_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure).'; source_paths=['distributions/distribution/profiles_2d/pressure_fast_parallel', 'edge_profiles/ggd/ion/pressure_fast_parallel/values', 'edge_profiles/ggd/electrons/pressure_fast_parallel/values', 'distributions/distribution/profiles_1d/pressure_fast_parallel', 'edge_profiles/ggd/neutral/pressure_fast_parallel/values', 'edge_profiles/ggd/pressure_parallel/values']

documentation='Poloidal current density due to parallel viscosity is the component along the poloidal basis direction of the electric current-density contribution generated by parallel viscous stress in a magnetized plasma. The projection is taken along \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta\), the unit tangent in the direction of increasing poloidal angle \(\theta\) at fixed radial flux label \(\rho\) and toroidal angle \(\phi\) in the flux-coordinate system \((\rho,\theta,\phi)\).

The component is the projection of the parallel-viscosity current-density vector onto that poloidal tangent:

$$
J_{\Pi_\parallel,\theta}
= \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta \cdot \left[
J_{\Pi_\parallel,\parallel}\,\hat{\mathbf{b}}
+ \frac{\mathbf{B} \times (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel)}{B^2}
\right]
$$

where \(J_{\Pi_\parallel,\theta}\) is the poloidal current density due to parallel viscosity, \(J_{\Pi_\parallel,\parallel}\) is the signed field-aligned projection of the same current-density contribution, \(\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/B\) is the magnetic-field unit vector, \(\mathbf{B}\) is the magnetic field, \(B=|\mathbf{B}|\), \(\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel\) is the parallel viscous stress tensor, and \(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel\) is the corresponding viscous force density. The cross-product term is the perpendicular force-balance drift contribution associated with the parallel-viscous force density.

This quantity is one directional projection of [current density due to parallel viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity). Other projections of the same contribution include [parallel current density due to parallel viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity), [radial current density due to parallel viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) along \(\hat{R}\), [toroidal current density due to parallel viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) along \(\hat{\phi}\), and [vertical current density due to parallel viscosity](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) along \(+\hat{Z}\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R,\phi,Z)\) frame, where \(R\) is major radius, \(\phi\) is toroidal angle, and \(Z\) is vertical height. It is distinct from [poloidal current density due to perpendicular viscosity](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity), which uses the perpendicular-viscous stress contribution rather than \(\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel\).

Sign convention: Positive when the current-density contribution points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle \(\theta\) in the flux-coordinate system \((\rho,\theta,\phi)\).'; documentation='Poloidal current density due to parallel viscosity is the component along the poloidal basis direction of the electric current-density contribution generated by parallel viscous stress in a magnetized plasma. The projection is taken along \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta\), the unit tangent in the direction of increasing poloidal angle \(\theta\) at fixed radial flux label \(\rho\) and toroidal angle \(\phi\) in the flux-coordinate system \((\rho,\theta,\phi)\).

The component is the projection of the parallel-viscosity current-density vector onto that poloidal tangent:

$$
J_{\Pi_\parallel,\theta}
= \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta \cdot \left[
J_{\Pi_\parallel,\parallel}\,\hat{\mathbf{b}}
+ \frac{\mathbf{B} \times (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel)}{B^2}
\right]
$$

where \(J_{\Pi_\parallel,\theta}\) is the poloidal current density due to parallel viscosity, \(J_{\Pi_\parallel,\parallel}\) is the signed field-aligned projection of the same current-density contribution, \(\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/B\) is the magnetic-field unit vector, \(\mathbf{B}\) is the magnetic field, \(B=|\mathbf{B}|\), \(\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel\) is the parallel viscous stress tensor, and \(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel\) is the corresponding viscous force density. The cross-product term is the perpendicular force-balance drift contribution associated with the parallel-viscous force density.

This quantity is one directional projection of [current density due to parallel viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity). Other projections of the same contribution include [parallel current density due to parallel viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity), [radial current density due to parallel viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) along \(\hat{R}\), [toroidal current density due to parallel viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) along \(\hat{\phi}\), and [vertical current density due to parallel viscosity](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) along \(+\hat{Z}\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R,\phi,Z)\) frame, where \(R\) is major radius, \(\phi\) is toroidal angle, and \(Z\) is vertical height. documentation='The resistance of a non-axisymmetric correction-coil conductor is the proportionality between its steady conventional current and the associated ohmic voltage drop. It describes dissipation in the conductor rather than inductive or other reactive voltage contributions.

For a uniform conductor, the resistance is defined by

$$
R = \rho \frac{L}{A}
$$

where $R$ is resistance in ohms, $\rho$ is electrical resistivity in ohm-meters, $L$ is the effective conductor length in meters, and $A$ is the cross-sectional area in square meters. The terminal relation is $V = IR$, where $V$ is the ohmic voltage drop and $I$ is the current; the corresponding resistive power is $P = I^2R$. The current is the [current of the correction coil], and the conductor area is represented by the [area of the correction coil](name:area_of_correction_coil).'; unit='ohm'

documentation='Vertical projection of the current density due to ion inertia is the electric-current component generated by inertial acceleration terms in the ion-fluid momentum equation. It includes the $Z$ component of the polarization-type current associated with finite ion mass and time-dependent or convective ion-fluid acceleration, taken along $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The vertical component is the projection of the ion-inertia current density vector onto $\hat{Z}$:

$$
J_{Z,\mathrm{inertia}} = \hat{Z}\cdot \left(\frac{m_i n_i}{B^2}\mathbf{B}\times \frac{d_i\mathbf{v}_i}{dt}\right)
$$

where $J_{Z,\mathrm{inertia}}$ is the vertical projection, $m_i$ is the ion mass, $n_i$ is the ion number density, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, $B=|\mathbf{B}|$, $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the ion-fluid velocity, and $d_i/dt=\partial/\partial t+\mathbf{v}_i\cdot\nabla$ is the ion convective derivative.

This quantity is the $Z$ projection of [current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:current_density_due_to_ion_inertia), not the full vector, its magnitude, or its divergence. The matched right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ components are [radial_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:radial_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia), [toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia), and this vertical projection; the field-aligned projection is [parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia). It excludes turbulent or anomalous-transport contributions such as [vertical_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport).

$$
\Gamma_{E,\theta}=-D^{\mathrm{eff}}_{E,\theta}\left.\frac{\partial e_{n,s}}{\partial \ell_\theta}\right|_{\rho,\phi}
$$

Here $\Gamma_{E,\theta}$ is the poloidal energy flux, $D^{\mathrm{eff}}_{E,\theta}$ is this diffusivity, $e_{n,s}$ is the energy density of neutral particles in internal state $s$, and $\ell_\theta$ is distance along the poloidal tangent. The coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ are the flux-surface, poloidal-angle, and toroidal-angle coordinates; the derivative is taken at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$.

This effective coefficient represents the net phenomenological response, not a single microscopic mechanism. $$

$$
\zeta_{lo} = 1 - \frac{2}{n_{lo}}
$$

Positive values indicate that the lower-outboard boundary corner lies outside the reference ellipse at the corresponding corner location, giving a more rectangular boundary; $\zeta_{lo}=0$ indicates the reference ellipse; negative values indicate that the corner lies inside the reference ellipse, giving inward concavity relative to that ellipse. documentation='Toroidal fast-particle torque due to collisions is the volume-integrated toroidal torque exerted on the fast, non-thermal particle population by Coulomb collisions with the thermal background plasma. It is the component of collisional angular-momentum transfer about the symmetry axis associated with increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The aggregate torque is defined as the plasma-volume integral of the toroidal collisional force density weighted by the major radius:

$$
T_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \int_V R \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} f_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}\leftarrow j}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $T_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the toroidal fast-particle torque due to collisions, $V$ is the plasma volume, $dV$ is a differential volume element, $\mathcal{B}$ is the set of thermal-background collision partners, and $f_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}\leftarrow j}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the toroidal component of the collisional force density exerted on fast, non-thermal particles by partner $j$.

The set $\mathcal{B}$ contains thermal electrons and every thermal ion species and every charge state of each thermal ion species; the ion part is charge-state-summed. This quantity is the aggregate over those collision partners, not an electron-only or charge-state-resolved contribution; the [thermal-electron collision contribution] and the [thermal-ion charge-state collision contribution](name:toroidal_fast_ion_charge_state_torque_due_to_collisions) sum to it when defined over the same volume and fast-particle population. It is the component of collisional angular-momentum transfer about the symmetry axis associated with increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The aggregate torque is defined as the plasma-volume integral of the toroidal collisional force density weighted by the major radius:

$$
T_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \int_V R \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}} f_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}\leftarrow j}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $T_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the toroidal fast-particle torque due to collisions, $V$ is the plasma volume, $dV$ is a differential volume element, $\mathcal{B}$ is the set of thermal-background collision partners, and $f_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}\leftarrow j}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the toroidal component of the collisional force density exerted on fast, non-thermal particles by partner $j$.

The set $\mathcal{B}$ contains thermal electrons and every thermal ion species and every charge state of each thermal ion species; the ion part is charge-state-summed. This quantity is the aggregate over those collision partners, not an electron-only or charge-state-resolved contribution; the [thermal-electron collision contribution] and the [thermal-ion charge-state collision contribution](name:toroidal_fast_ion_charge_state_torque_due_to_collisions) sum to it when defined over the same volume and fast-particle population. The equal-and-opposite collisional angular-momentum transfer to the thermal background is represented by the [thermal-electron](name:toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_due_to_collisions) and [thermal-ion](name:toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_due_to_collisions) reaction channels.

Sign convention: Positive when Coulomb collisions exert a net toroidal force on fast, non-thermal particles in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.'; source_paths=['distributions/distribution/global_quantities/collisions/ion/torque_fast_phi']

documentation='Neon density at a limiter is the local number density of neon ions in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface. The evaluation point is the plasma side of the magnetic presheath or sheath entrance at the limiter contact, not the magnetic separatrix, consistent with the parent [density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter).

Unless a charge-state-resolved quantity specifies a particular ionization stage, this density is summed over all positive neon charge states ($\mathrm{Ne}^{1+}$ through $\mathrm{Ne}^{10+}$):

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ne}} = \sum_{z=1}^{10} n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{z+}}$ is the partial number density of neon ions in charge state $z$.

Neon is introduced as a controlled radiative impurity for power exhaust and divertor detachment. At the limiter, the local neon density governs recycling fluxes, charge-exchange with neutral neon, and impurity-driven edge plasma cooling near the wall. $$
F_{c\ell} = C_{\ell R} F_{R,c} + C_{\ell Z} F_{Z,c}
$$

documentation='In multi-fluid edge plasma transport models, gradient-driven diffusive closures can produce toroidal momentum-flux densities that exceed the physically realizable collisionless free-streaming limit in steep-gradient regions. A toroidal momentum-flux-limiter coefficient $\alpha_{m,\phi}$ is introduced to bound the effective $\hat{\phi}$-projected momentum-flux density, where $m$ denotes momentum and $\phi$ denotes the toroidal projection. The toroidal projection is along $\hat{\phi}$, the tangent to increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$ and $\hat{R} \times \hat{\phi} = \hat{Z}$.

The bounded toroidal momentum-flux density satisfies the limiter constraint:

$$
|\Pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{lim}}| \le \alpha_{m,\phi}\,\Pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{FS}}
$$

where $\Pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{lim}}$ is the limited toroidal momentum-flux density, $\Pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{FS}}$ is the toroidal free-streaming momentum-flux reference scale, and $\alpha_{m,\phi}$ is the toroidal momentum-flux-limiter coefficient.

This coefficient is the toroidal directional specialization of [momentum-flux-limiter coefficient](name:momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient), not a particle-, heat-, or energy-flux limiter and not the momentum-flux density itself. It is intrinsically non-negative: it caps the magnitude of the modeled toroidal momentum-flux density and does not carry the positive or negative sign of that flux. documentation='Radial ion charge-state diffusivity is the effective Fickian particle diffusivity for ions in a specified ionization state along the radial direction. It is the scalar transport coefficient that relates the radial diffusive particle flux density of that charge state to the negative radial gradient of its number density.

For the radial projection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the defining Fickian relation is:

$$
\Gamma^{\mathrm{diff}}_{s,R} = -D_{s,R}\,\nabla_R n_s
$$

where $\Gamma^{\mathrm{diff}}_{s,R}$ is the radial diffusive particle flux density of charge state $s$, $D_{s,R}$ is this diffusivity, $n_s$ is the number density of charge state $s$, and $\nabla_R n_s = \hat{\mathbf{R}}\cdot\nabla n_s$ is its derivative along increasing $R$.

documentation='The radial neutral-state momentum coefficient is a dimensionless flux-limiter factor assigned to a specified neutral particle state—atomic, molecular, or excitation—in edge-plasma transport closures. It scales the free-streaming bound on the radial component of momentum-flux density while preserving the direction of the modeled flux.

The defining relation for the radial projection is:

$$
\Pi_R = c_R \cdot \Pi_R^{\rm FS}
$$

where $\Pi_R$ is the modeled momentum-flux-density component projected onto the radial unit vector $\hat{R}$, $\Pi_R^{\rm FS}$ is its free-streaming bound, $c_R$ is the radial dimensionless coefficient, and the subscript $R$ denotes the radial direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Here, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $\hat{R}$ is the corresponding radial unit vector. When flux limiting is active, $c_R$ lies between zero and one.

This quantity applies to one specified neutral particle state in edge-plasma transport closures and is not summed over distinct neutral species or internal states. It represents only the radial component and is not the full neutral-state momentum coefficient or the momentum-flux density itself.

It is the radial component of the vector [neutral-state momentum flux-limiter coefficient](name:neutral_internal_state_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient_over_edge_region). The [poloidal neutral-state momentum flux-limiter coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_state_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient) and [vertical neutral-state momentum flux-limiter coefficient](name:vertical_neutral_state_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient) provide analogous directional factors for their respective projections.'; source_paths=['plasma_transport/model/ggd/neutral/state/momentum/flux_limiter/radial', 'plasma_transport/model/profiles_1d/neutral/state/momentum/flux_limiter/radial', 'edge_transport/model/ggd/neutral/state/momentum/flux_limiter/radial']

documentation='The total magnetic-field magnitude is the nonnegative Euclidean norm of the local magnetic-induction vector at the pressure-pedestal top on the high-field side. It represents the complete field at that location rather than a selected directional component.

The defining relation is

$$
B = |\mathbf{B}| = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_\phi^2 + B_Z^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-induction vector, $B$ is its magnitude, and $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are its signed projections onto the right-handed cylindrical basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity is evaluated locally at the high-field-side pressure-pedestal top and includes all magnetic-field components through the Euclidean norm. It excludes component-specific or perturbation-only fields and is not a signed projection. documentation="This quantity is the coefficient of total ion particle density in the implicit part of the total ion particle source term. It represents the stiff, primary-quantity-dependent contribution separated from the source term's explicit part.

The implicit source contribution is defined by

$$
S_{i,\mathrm{imp}} = \alpha_{i,\mathrm{imp}} n_i
$$

where $S_{i,\mathrm{imp}}$ is the implicit contribution to the total ion particle source, $\alpha_{i,\mathrm{imp}}$ is this source-rate coefficient, and $n_i$ is the total ion particle density.

The quantity applies to the aggregate ion population, with the total ion density and corresponding source contribution summed over the included ion species and charge states. It is a scalar coefficient for the particle channel, not the complete particle source and not the explicit, primary-quantity-independent contribution.

Its role is analogous to the coefficient in [implicit electron particle source rate](name:implicit_electron_particle_source_rate), while [implicit ion energy source rate](name:implicit_ion_energy_source_rate) applies the same implicit decomposition to the ion energy channel. documentation='Radial component of the effective convective velocity used for ion particle transport is the scalar transport velocity whose multiplication by ion particle density gives the advective part of the ion particle flux in the radial direction. The defining relation for the radial convective contribution to the ion particle flux is:

$$
\Gamma_{i,R}^{\mathrm{conv}} = n_i v_{i,R}^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $\Gamma_{i,R}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the radial convective ion particle flux, $n_i$ is the ion particle density, and $v_{i,R}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the radial ion particle convection velocity.

The quantity applies to collective ion particle transport in the edge plasma and to the ion species as a whole. Because velocity is an intensive per-particle field, the species-level ion value is the density-weighted mean over all ion charge states; if $q$ indexes ion charge state, $v_{i,q,R}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the radial convection velocity of charge state $q$, and $n_{i,q}$ is its particle density, then $v_{i,R}^{\mathrm{conv}} = (\sum_q n_{i,q} v_{i,q,R}^{\mathrm{conv}})/(\sum_q n_{i,q})$.
